purpose: Every corpus case where `node bin/vibe.js check` disagrees with the case's declared expectation. The conformance runner measures two BACKENDS; neither is the shipped CLI, so this file is the written record of how far the product is from the contract the corpus is quoted as stating. `direction` product-accepts is the dangerous one — the corpus requires a refusal and the product compiled it. `verdict` says which side is wrong; `decision-needed` rows may not be moved by either side until the decisions ledger owner settles them. A row disappears when the divergence is FIXED, never when it is tolerated.

divergences.note: src/cli.ts:753-777 runs buildRelativeRuntimeGraph before the semantic stage and returns as soon as it has anything to say. Here it does not even produce a diagnostic: it throws a TypeError that backendFailure (src/cli.ts:1418-1432) turns into a code-less, position-less VIBELANG_PROJECT_ERROR, so the rule the corpus pins is never reached. Both sides refuse the program, so this is a diagnostic-identity divergence, not a safety hole. The corpus states the contract correctly; the fix is for the graph to defer an edge it cannot resolve to the semantic stage instead of aborting the run.

The semantic rule (poc/src/language/semantic.ts:5409-5439) anchors it on the import SPECIFIER in the authored .vibe, which is the position the corpus pins. src/relative-runtime-graph.ts:946-961 re-implements the same contract code with a different message and deliberately anchors it at the FOREIGN module's first statement (parsed.statements[0]), in a file the author may not own. The CLI reaches the graph first and returns immediately, so the graph's spelling is the only one a user ever sees, and every diagnostic the semantic stage would have paired with it (the VIBE1301/VIBE1302 for the Result the untrusted call discards) is suppressed along with it. That suppression-behind-a-refused-module-edge is the exact shape this corpus retired from the Go fork on 2026-08-25 (see the notes on foreign-module-without-a-trust-marker); it is still live in the shipped CLI. The corpus is right on both the position and the pairing.

ADDED 2026-08-27 with the reached-module-closure fix. Twelfth row in this bucket and the same cause: `VIBE1510` has two independent implementations -- `poc/src/language/semantic.ts` reports at the authored `.vibe` import site (column 24 here), while the CLI's `src/relative-runtime-graph.ts` walks the graph and reports at the reached foreign module's own first statement. Both refuse; only the position differs, and product-ACCEPTS stays 0. WHAT THESE THREE CASES ARE: until this fix, a foreign module reached at depth >= 2 was never checked for the module-initialization trust marker by EITHER semantic pass -- `checkForeignModuleInitializers` and the fork's `checkForeignModuleTrust` both iterated only the authored file's own statements. Measured with a runtime oracle, an unmarked module behind a properly marked relay compiled clean and RAN its initializer at depths 2 through 5, through cycles and diamonds. The product was already covered, by the CLI graph alone; the language rule was not, which is why no corpus case could be written before and why these three could only land once both backends walked the closure.

ADDED 2026-08-27, and its ABSENCE was the interesting part. This case was not listed before, which read as agreement between the product and the corpus. It was agreement for a stale reason: the CLI's runtime graph carried its own case-INSENSITIVE copy of the trust-marker predicate (src/relative-runtime-graph.ts:362-363 had /i where the other three implementations deliberately do not), so it ACCEPTED all three miscased modules, and the separate semantic pass refused at the .vibe import site -- which happens to be the position the corpus declares. Right answer, wrong mechanism: moving the untrusted module one edge further away made the rule disappear entirely, and a runtime oracle measured an untrusted foreign initializer executing on a program reporting ok: true. With the /i flags removed the graph now refuses on its own, at the foreign module's own position rather than at the authored import site, so the case joins the sibling row `near-miss-trust-markers-do-not-confer-module-trust` it always belonged beside. Both sides refuse; the positions differ because VIBE1510 still has two independent implementations (poc/src/language/semantic.ts and src/relative-runtime-graph.ts), which is recorded as a known-open item entangled with the dynamic-import decision. product-ACCEPTS remains 0.
